courses.title: Sleep & Circadian Rhythm
courses.tagline: Protect the crew's internal clock, alertness, and performance.
introduction: Sleep is not downtime. It is an active biological process that supports memory, mood, immune function, metabolism, and the ability to make safe decisions. In space, the usual cues that shape sleep are disrupted.
This course explores the station sleep environment, the circadian system, fatigue risk, countermeasures, and the operational skill of building a crew sleep plan.
objectives: Explain why sleep is an operational safety system in spaceflight.
Describe how light, schedule, noise, and workload influence circadian rhythm.
Recognize signs of cumulative fatigue and explain why self-report alone is not enough.
Build a qualitative crew sleep and fatigue plan that protects performance.

modules.title: The Sleep Environment in Space
modules.summary: Why sleeping in orbit is different, and what the crew sleep station is designed to control.

lessons.title: A Day Without a Normal Day
content: The International Space Station orbits Earth roughly every 90 minutes, so the crew experiences many sunrises and sunsets during a 24-hour period. The body still carries an approximately 24-hour internal clock, but the light-dark pattern around the crew no longer matches it.

Crew schedules use a mission timeline to create a consistent work and rest rhythm. Sleep stations provide a restrained sleeping bag, controlled light, airflow, and a quieter place to rest. These are engineered aids, not a cure for a schedule that does not protect sleep.
lessons.key_takeaway: Orbital light patterns are not a normal day-night cycle, so sleep must be protected by design.

lessons.title: Why Sleep Matters
content: Sleep supports attention, working memory, emotional regulation, immune function, and metabolism. When sleep is restricted, people often notice irritability and slower reactions before they notice a decline in complex decision-making.
In a hazardous environment, a sleepy crew member may be less able to monitor systems, catch errors, or communicate clearly. That makes sleep a crew safety topic, not a personal preference.
lessons.key_takeaway: Sleep protects both the individual and the team's ability to operate safely.

key_points: The station's orbital light pattern does not provide a normal 24-hour day.
Sleep stations control light, noise, airflow, and body restraint.
Sleep supports attention, mood, memory, immune function, and metabolism.

practical_activity.title: Audit Your Sleep Environment
practical_activity.prompt: List three things in your sleep environment that affect rest, then choose one realistic change to test for a week.
steps: Record light, noise, temperature, and screen use before bed.
Identify the factor most likely to delay sleep.
Choose one change and describe how you will know whether it helped.

questions.question: Why is sleep scheduling on the space station different from a typical home schedule?
options: The station has no clocks
The orbit produces frequent light-dark changes that do not match a normal day
Crew members do not need sleep in space
The station is always completely dark
questions.explanation: The station orbits Earth about every 90 minutes, creating many sunrises and sunsets. The schedule and lighting must compensate for this.

questions.question: What is a primary purpose of a crew sleep station?
options: To provide a place for equipment storage
To control light, noise, airflow, and body restraint during rest
To replace the need for a sleep schedule
To keep the crew awake for monitoring
questions.explanation: A sleep station creates a controlled rest environment. It does not replace the need for a protected sleep opportunity.

questions.question: Which set of signs most suggests accumulated fatigue?
options: Improved reaction time and increased patience
Slower reactions, irritability, and difficulty concentrating
A sudden interest in extra exercise
Consistently feeling rested after short sleep
questions.explanation: Slower reactions, irritability, and concentration problems are common fatigue signs. They deserve follow-up, not dismissal.

questions.question: What is the strongest first response when a crew member reports persistent fatigue?
options: Tell them to ignore it until the mission ends
Protect sleep opportunity, review workload, and check in again
Increase their task load to build stamina
Give them a stimulant and take no other action
questions.explanation: Fatigue is managed by addressing sleep opportunity and workload, then monitoring. Stimulants are not a substitute for recovery.

modules.title: Circadian Rhythm and Light
modules.summary: How the internal clock works and how light can be used as an operational tool.

lessons.title: The Body's Internal Clock
content: The circadian system organizes sleep, alertness, body temperature, hormone release, and metabolism across roughly 24 hours. Light is the strongest external cue that keeps this system aligned with the day.

In orbit, the crew may see bright sunlight at unusual times. Misalignment between the internal clock and the work schedule can make it harder to fall asleep, stay asleep, and feel alert at the right moments.
lessons.key_takeaway: Light is the main cue that keeps the circadian system aligned with the work schedule.

lessons.title: Lighting as a Tool
content: A well-designed lighting plan provides bright light during the active period and dims it before sleep. Consistent wake times, a predictable wind-down, and reduced screen exposure can support the same rhythm.
Lighting is not the only factor. Noise, temperature, workload, and stress also shape sleep. A useful plan combines several small controls instead of relying on one intervention.
lessons.key_takeaway: Bright active-period light plus a dim, predictable wind-down supports better rest.

key_points: The circadian system influences sleep, alertness, temperature, hormones, and metabolism.
Light timing is more useful than light intensity alone.
A sleep plan should combine lighting, schedule, noise, temperature, and workload controls.

practical_activity.title: Build a Light and Wind-Down Plan
practical_activity.prompt: Design a two-hour wind-down routine that reduces bright light and screen use before sleep.
steps: Choose a consistent sleep and wake anchor.
Plan one hour of dim light and one hour of low-stimulation activity.
Identify the screen or communication habit you will move earlier.

questions.question: What is the strongest external cue for the human circadian system?
options: Sound
Light
Room shape
Exercise only
questions.explanation: Light exposure, especially its timing, is the dominant cue that aligns the circadian system.

questions.question: Which lighting pattern best supports a normal sleep-wake rhythm?
options: Bright light all night and dim light all day
Bright light during the active period and dim light before sleep
No light at any time
Random changes in light throughout the day
questions.explanation: A consistent bright active period and a dim wind-down support circadian alignment.

questions.question: Why is a consistent wake time useful?
options: It removes the need for sleep
It helps anchor the circadian rhythm and the sleep-wake cycle
It guarantees perfect sleep in space
It replaces the need for lighting control
questions.explanation: A regular wake time is an anchor for the circadian system, though it works best with other controls.

questions.question: A crew member uses a bright tablet late into the sleep period. What is the most likely concern?
options: The tablet will damage station power
Bright light near sleep can delay the body's sleep signal
It will immediately cause dehydration
It has no effect on sleep
questions.explanation: Bright light close to sleep can make it harder to settle. Moving screen use earlier is a practical countermeasure.

modules.title: Sleep Debt, Fatigue, and Performance
modules.summary: How small sleep losses accumulate into operational risk.

lessons.title: Sleep Debt Is Cumulative
content: Sleep debt builds when a person repeatedly gets less sleep than needed. A single long sleep can help, but it may not fully restore performance after several restricted nights.

The effects can be subtle: a person may feel functional while their attention, reaction time, and error detection are reduced. This is why fatigue management cannot rely only on how the crew says they feel.
lessons.key_takeaway: Several short nights can create risk that a single recovery sleep does not fully erase.

lessons.title: Recognizing Fatigue in a Crew
content: Useful fatigue indicators include slower responses, missed steps, irritability, withdrawn communication, and unusual difficulty with routine tasks. A change from a person's normal behavior is a meaningful signal.
Team members should feel able to report fatigue without blame. A no-blame report followed by a practical adjustment is safer than waiting for an error to reveal the problem.
lessons.key_takeaway: Watch for changes in performance and behavior, and make fatigue reporting safe.

key_points: Sleep debt accumulates across days.
Fatigue can impair performance before a person notices it.
Behavior change, missed steps, and irritability are operational signals.
Reporting fatigue should lead to support, not punishment.

practical_activity.title: Fatigue Signal Checklist
practical_activity.prompt: Create a short checklist a team could use to notice fatigue without diagnosing a medical condition.
steps: Choose three observable behaviors, such as missed steps or shortened communication.
Add one question that invites a crew member to report fatigue.
Describe one immediate, low-risk adjustment.

questions.question: What does sleep debt mean?
options: A crew member owes the station money
The cumulative effect of getting less sleep than needed over time
A single night of poor sleep with no lasting effect
A measure of station power use
questions.explanation: Sleep debt is cumulative. Repeated short sleep can create performance risk even if the person feels used to it.

questions.question: Why should a fatigue plan not rely only on self-report?
options: Crew members always lie
Fatigue can reduce self-awareness and judgment
Self-report is illegal in space
Only machines can detect sleep
questions.explanation: Fatigue can impair the ability to judge one's own performance. Observable behavior and team check-ins add useful information.

questions.question: Which is the most useful operational response to a fatigue report?
options: Record it and take no action
Review sleep opportunity and workload, then adjust and follow up
Assign extra tasks to test alertness
Tell the crew member to keep it private
questions.explanation: The response should reduce risk through schedule and workload adjustments, with follow-up.

questions.question: A crew member who is usually talkative becomes quiet and makes a repeated checklist error. What should the team consider?
options: Only a personality change with no safety relevance
A possible fatigue or workload signal worth checking
A reason to remove all their responsibilities immediately
Evidence that the checklist is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Behavior change plus a repeated error is a signal to check in and review workload, not to ignore or immediately punish.

modules.title: Fatigue Countermeasures
modules.summary: Practical ways to support alertness and recovery within an operational schedule.

lessons.title: Sleep Hygiene in Orbit
content: Sleep hygiene is a set of habits that make rest more likely: a consistent schedule, a wind-down routine, a dark and quiet sleep area, and attention to caffeine timing. In orbit, each habit must be adapted to the station environment.

Caffeine can improve short-term alertness, but it can also make sleep harder if used too late. The useful question is not only whether caffeine helps now, but whether it protects the next sleep opportunity.
lessons.key_takeaway: Countermeasures should protect the next sleep opportunity, not just the current shift.

lessons.title: Naps, Workload, and Chronotype
content: A short planned nap can improve alertness during a long operational period. It works best as a supplement to core sleep, not a replacement for it. Nap timing and length matter, and individual preferences vary.

Chronotype describes whether a person tends to feel more alert earlier or later in the day. A crew schedule does not need to accommodate every preference, but awareness helps the team place demanding tasks at sensible times.
lessons.key_takeaway: Naps and schedule timing are supporting tools, while protected core sleep remains the foundation.

key_points: Consistent schedule and wind-down habits support sleep.
Caffeine timing should protect, not undermine, the next sleep period.
Short naps can supplement core sleep but should not replace it.
Chronotype awareness can improve task timing.

practical_activity.title: Design a Fatigue Countermeasure Menu
practical_activity.prompt: Create a menu of three countermeasures for a tired crew, including when each is appropriate and when it is not.
steps: Choose one schedule control, one rest control, and one environment control.
State the best time to use each.
State one situation where the countermeasure would be insufficient.

questions.question: What is the best use of a short nap during a long mission day?
options: Replace the main sleep period entirely
Supplement alertness while still protecting core sleep
Replace all fatigue reporting
Guarantee perfect performance for the rest of the mission
questions.explanation: A short nap can support alertness, but it does not replace the need for adequate core sleep.

questions.question: Why does caffeine timing matter?
options: Caffeine only works in the morning
Late caffeine can make it harder to fall asleep and protect the next sleep opportunity
Caffeine replaces sleep
Caffeine has no effect on sleep
questions.explanation: Caffeine can improve short-term alertness but may interfere with sleep if used too close to rest.

questions.question: What is chronotype?
options: A station exercise machine
A person's tendency toward earlier or later alertness across the day
A type of radiation shield
A method for measuring water recovery
questions.explanation: Chronotype describes individual differences in daily timing. It can inform schedule design but is not a diagnosis.

questions.question: Which combination best supports a tired crew member?
options: More caffeine, less sleep, and more tasks
Protected sleep, a realistic workload, and a follow-up check
A nap and no schedule change
Ignore the report until the final assessment
questions.explanation: The strongest support combines recovery, workload adjustment, and follow-up.

modules.title: Monitoring Sleep and Crew Scheduling
modules.summary: How to use qualitative sleep information to build a safer schedule.

lessons.title: Sleep Logs and Wearable Data
content: Sleep logs capture bedtimes, wake times, rest quality, and fatigue reports. Wearables can add activity and rest patterns. Together they help the team spot trends that a single conversation might miss.
These tools are not a diagnosis. Their operational value is to prompt a conversation, support schedule changes, and document whether a change helped. Privacy and crew trust matter.
lessons.key_takeaway: Sleep monitoring is most useful as a trend-and-conversation tool, not as a label.

lessons.title: Building a Crew Sleep Plan
content: A good crew sleep plan protects a consistent sleep opportunity, coordinates handovers, manages light and noise, and places demanding tasks where the crew is most likely to be alert. It also says what to do when fatigue is reported.
The plan should be simple enough to follow during a busy mission. Build in a review point, because a schedule that works on Day 1 may not work after several days of workload.
lessons.key_takeaway: A workable sleep plan coordinates the whole crew and includes a review and response process.

key_points: Sleep logs and wearables reveal trends but do not diagnose.
A sleep plan should protect a consistent window and coordinate handovers.
Demanding tasks should be placed with alertness in mind.
Every sleep plan needs a review and fatigue-response process.

practical_activity.title: Crew Sleep Plan Draft
practical_activity.prompt: Draft a one-day crew sleep plan with a protected sleep window, handover times, a lighting plan, and a fatigue check-in.
steps: Set a consistent sleep and wake anchor.
Place the handover so it does not fragment the sleep window.
Add one lighting control and one check-in question.
Name one trigger for adjusting the plan.

questions.question: What is the best operational use of a crew sleep log?
options: To diagnose a sleep disorder without medical support
To identify trends, prompt a conversation, and evaluate schedule changes
To replace all crew check-ins
To rank crew members
questions.explanation: Logs help identify trends and support decisions. They are not a standalone diagnosis.

questions.question: Which schedule design best protects sleep?
options: Frequent handovers throughout the sleep window
A consistent protected sleep window with coordinated handovers
A different sleep time every day
Bright light during the entire rest period
questions.explanation: Consistency and protection of the sleep window are foundational, with handovers planned around it.

questions.question: Why should a sleep plan include a review point?
options: Because sleep needs never change
Because workload and conditions change, and the plan may need adjustment
To create more paperwork
Because the first plan is always wrong
questions.explanation: A review keeps the plan responsive to changing workload and crew reports.

questions.question: Which is the strongest fatigue-response process?
options: Wait for an error, then investigate
Encourage reporting, assess workload and sleep, adjust, and follow up
Ask the crew to hide fatigue to protect morale
Use caffeine for every report
questions.explanation: A safe process makes reporting easy and responds with practical changes and follow-up.

practical_activity.title: Design a 24-Hour Crew Sleep Plan
practical_activity.description: Create a sleep and fatigue plan for a four-person crew during a busy station operations day. Use qualitative reasoning: you do not need to invent clinical measurements.
steps: Define a consistent sleep and wake anchor for the crew.
Place handovers, communication, and demanding tasks around the protected sleep window.
Describe the lighting and noise controls for the wind-down period.
Include a fatigue check-in and a rule for adjusting the schedule.
Explain one trade-off between mission tasks and crew rest.
practical_activity.submission_prompt: Paste your plan and a short rationale. Explain how it protects alertness and what you would change if the crew reported persistent fatigue.

questions.question: A crew has had three nights of shortened sleep. Performance is still acceptable, but two members report irritability. What is the best operational interpretation?
options: There is no risk because performance is acceptable
The reports may signal cumulative fatigue that deserves a schedule and workload review
The crew should be given more tasks to stay awake
The reports are irrelevant to safety
questions.explanation: Cumulative fatigue can affect performance before it is obvious. Irritability and reduced sleep are signals to review and support.

questions.question: Which change is most likely to support circadian alignment during a station mission?
options: Randomize sleep times to match the orbit
Use bright light during the active period and dim light before sleep, with a consistent schedule
Keep all lights bright at all times
Remove all clocks from the station
questions.explanation: Consistent timing and appropriate light exposure are core circadian supports.

questions.question: Why is a no-blame fatigue report valuable?
options: It eliminates the need for sleep
It surfaces risk early so the team can adjust before an error occurs
It proves the crew is unfit
It replaces medical care
questions.explanation: Early reporting enables practical risk reduction. Blame discourages reporting and hides risk.

questions.question: A short nap is proposed for a tired crew member before a demanding task. What is the best guidance?
options: Use the nap as a complete replacement for the main sleep period
Use a short planned nap as a supplement, and still protect core sleep
Avoid all naps under every circumstance
Use the nap and skip the fatigue check-in
questions.explanation: Naps can support alertness but do not replace core sleep. Follow-up remains important.

questions.question: Which statement about sleep monitoring is most accurate?
options: A wearable diagnosis is always correct
Logs and wearables are useful trend tools but not a substitute for medical assessment
Sleep logs should be used to punish crew members
Monitoring removes the need for a sleep plan
questions.explanation: Monitoring supports awareness and operational decisions. It does not replace clinical assessment.

questions.question: What makes a crew sleep plan operationally strong?
options: It protects sleep, coordinates the team, places demanding tasks sensibly, and includes review and response
It maximizes task time by removing all rest
It relies on a single countermeasure
It is written once and never reviewed
questions.explanation: A strong plan integrates protection, coordination, task timing, and a review process.

courses.title: Physical Health & Exercise
courses.tagline: Use exercise to defend bone, muscle, heart, and mission capability.
introduction: In microgravity, the body no longer receives the same mechanical loading from standing, walking, and carrying weight. Without a countermeasure, bone and muscle can lose strength and the cardiovascular system can decondition.
This course explains the physiology of unloading, the station exercise tools, how an exercise plan is built, and how crews prevent injury while staying fit.
objectives: Explain how reduced mechanical loading affects bone, muscle, and the cardiovascular system.
Identify the purpose of major station exercise devices.
Describe how frequency, intensity, time, type, and progression shape an exercise plan.
Apply safety and maintenance thinking to an equipment fault.

mission_links.label: Day 5 - Crew Health and Fitness Debrief

modules.title: Gravity, Loading, and the Body
modules.summary: Why the body needs mechanical load and what changes when gravity is no longer pulling.

lessons.title: The Load of Everyday Gravity
content: On Earth, standing, walking, climbing, and carrying objects load the skeleton and muscles. The body continually remodels tissue in response to that load. Gravity is a constant training stimulus, even when a person is not exercising.
In microgravity, that everyday loading is greatly reduced. The body adapts to what it experiences, so without a deliberate countermeasure, tissues and systems that depend on load can weaken.
lessons.key_takeaway: Gravity provides continuous loading on Earth; spaceflight requires a deliberate replacement.

lessons.title: A Whole-Body Adaptation
content: Unloading affects more than muscles. Bone remodeling, blood volume, heart function, balance, and sensorimotor coordination all respond to the changed environment. The body is efficient: it reduces capacity that is not being used.
Exercise is therefore not only about fitness or appearance. It is a multi-system countermeasure that supports mission capability and the return to gravity.
lessons.key_takeaway: Exercise protects multiple systems, not just muscle size.

key_points: Gravity provides continuous mechanical loading on Earth.
Microgravity reduces the load on bone and muscle.
The cardiovascular and sensorimotor systems also adapt.
Exercise is a multi-system countermeasure.

practical_activity.title: Map Your Daily Loading
practical_activity.prompt: List five everyday activities that load your bones or muscles, then explain how each would change in microgravity.
steps: Choose activities such as walking, climbing stairs, or carrying a bag.
Name the body areas that receive load.
Identify which station exercise could replace that stimulus.

questions.question: Why do bones and muscles weaken in microgravity without countermeasures?
options: The body receives less mechanical loading
There is no food in space
The crew sleeps too much
Gravity becomes stronger
questions.explanation: Tissue adapts to load. When loading is reduced, bone and muscle can lose capacity.

questions.question: Which is an example of everyday loading on Earth?
options: Floating without contact
Walking and carrying objects
Sleeping in a restrained bag
Watching a screen while weightless
questions.explanation: Weight-bearing and resistance from daily activity provide ongoing mechanical load.

questions.question: Why is exercise in space a multi-system countermeasure?
options: It only changes muscle size
It supports bone, muscle, cardiovascular, and sensorimotor health
It replaces all medical care
It removes the need for sleep
questions.explanation: Exercise contributes to several systems that adapt to unloading.

questions.question: What does the body tend to do in microgravity?
options: Maintain every capacity regardless of use
Reduce capacity that is not being loaded or used
Grow stronger without exercise
Lose all coordination immediately
questions.explanation: The body adapts to the demands placed on it. Reduced demand can lead to reduced capacity.

modules.title: Bone and Muscle in Microgravity
modules.summary: The physiology of bone remodeling and muscle maintenance during spaceflight.

lessons.title: Bone Remodeling
content: Bone is living tissue. Cells build new bone and remove old bone in a continuous remodeling process. Mechanical load is one signal that helps keep the balance toward maintaining bone mass and strength.

NASA research has documented bone loss during spaceflight, with estimates often described as roughly 1 to 1.5 percent of bone mass per month for some astronauts. Individual responses vary. The key operational point is that load-bearing exercise and nutrition are both part of protection.
lessons.key_takeaway: Bone responds to load and nutrition; spaceflight can shift the balance toward loss.

lessons.title: Muscle Maintenance
content: Muscles that are not used for resistance or postural support can lose mass and strength. In space, the legs may be used differently, and the back and postural muscles may not work against gravity in the same way.
Resistance exercise provides a loading stimulus. Aerobic exercise supports cardiovascular fitness. A complete plan includes both, rather than choosing one and ignoring the other.
lessons.key_takeaway: Resistance work supports muscle and bone; aerobic work supports the cardiovascular system.

key_points: Bone remodeling is influenced by mechanical load.
Spaceflight can cause bone loss, with individual variation.
Muscles lose mass and strength when loading is reduced.
A complete plan combines resistance and aerobic exercise.

practical_activity.title: Countermeasure Match
practical_activity.prompt: Match three body systems to an exercise approach that supports each, and explain the link.
steps: Choose bone, skeletal muscle, and the cardiovascular system.
Select a resistance or aerobic approach for each.
Explain why the approach provides the needed stimulus.

questions.question: What is bone remodeling?
options: A process where bone is continuously built and removed
A method of cleaning station filters
A sleep phase
A type of radiation shielding
questions.explanation: Bone is dynamic tissue. Remodeling balances formation and removal and responds to load and nutrition.

questions.question: Which exercise type is most directly associated with loading bone and muscle?
options: Resistance exercise
Passive observation
Sleeping
Listening to music
questions.explanation: Resistance exercise provides mechanical load that supports bone and muscle maintenance.

questions.question: Why is aerobic exercise still important if resistance work protects muscle?
options: It supports cardiovascular fitness and endurance
It replaces the need for sleep
It prevents all bone loss
It makes resistance exercise unnecessary
questions.explanation: Aerobic exercise supports the cardiovascular system and endurance. Both types are useful.

questions.question: What is a reasonable statement about bone loss in spaceflight?
options: It is identical for every astronaut
It can occur, varies among individuals, and is addressed through exercise and nutrition
It never happens
It is caused only by dehydration
questions.explanation: Bone loss is documented and variable. Countermeasures include exercise and nutrition, with individual medical monitoring.

modules.title: Exercise Hardware on Station
modules.summary: The purpose, setup, and safety logic of major space station exercise devices.

lessons.title: Resistance and Aerobic Devices
content: Station exercise hardware is designed for weightlessness. A resistance device can provide loaded exercise without relying on gravity. A treadmill uses a harness system to keep the crew member from floating away while walking or running.

A cycle ergometer provides aerobic exercise and can support different intensities. Each device has setup, restraint, and maintenance procedures. The crew trains on the equipment, but the equipment also needs inspection and care.
lessons.key_takeaway: Station exercise devices use restraints and engineered loading to replace what gravity normally provides.

lessons.title: Setup, Safety, and Maintenance
content: A safe session begins with correct setup: restraints, harness, seat, foot position, and the intended load. A device that feels different from normal is a signal to stop and report, not to force the session.

Maintenance is part of exercise readiness. A fault that is ignored can remove the device from service later, reduce exercise options, and create a schedule problem. Documenting the issue early protects the whole plan.
lessons.key_takeaway: Correct setup and prompt fault reporting protect both the crew member and the exercise capability.

key_points: Resistance devices provide engineered loading in weightlessness.
A treadmill harness keeps the crew member in position.
A cycle ergometer supports aerobic exercise.
Setup, restraint, fault reporting, and maintenance are part of safety.

practical_activity.title: Pre-Session Equipment Check
practical_activity.prompt: Create a five-item pre-session check for a station exercise device.
steps: Include restraints, setup, load, and the surrounding area.
Add one question that helps the crew member decide whether to stop.
Explain why each item matters.

questions.question: Why does a space station treadmill use a harness?
options: To keep the crew member from floating away and to provide load
To measure radiation
To recycle water
To replace the need for exercise
questions.explanation: The harness restrains the crew member and helps create a weight-bearing running or walking stimulus.

questions.question: What should a crew member do if an exercise device feels abnormal during a session?
options: Increase the load to test it
Stop, secure the device, and report the fault
Continue silently
Ask another crew member to use it first
questions.explanation: Suspected faults require stopping use and reporting. Continuing can increase injury or equipment risk.

questions.question: Why is maintenance part of exercise planning?
options: A neglected device can become unavailable and reduce exercise options
Maintenance replaces sleep
It makes exercise unnecessary
It only matters for appearance
questions.explanation: Equipment availability directly affects the exercise countermeasure plan.

questions.question: Which is a correct setup principle?
options: Skip restraints when the session is short
Use the intended restraints, setup, and load, and check the area before starting
Use the highest load on the first session
Ignore unusual sounds until the end of the week
questions.explanation: Consistent setup and restraint checks reduce risk and support a useful session.

modules.title: Exercise Prescription and Progression
modules.summary: How to build a balanced plan without inventing individualized medical prescriptions.

lessons.title: The Building Blocks
content: An exercise plan can be described by frequency, intensity, time, type, and progression. In space, the plan must also account for available equipment, crew time, and the need for both resistance and aerobic work.

NASA crew schedules commonly include about two hours per day for exercise and related setup, reflecting how important the countermeasure is. The exact plan is individualized and is not a universal prescription.
lessons.key_takeaway: A balanced plan uses recognized exercise principles and individual operational constraints.

lessons.title: Progression and Recovery
content: Progression means gradually increasing the challenge when the body is ready. Too little stimulus may not protect capacity; too much too quickly can cause injury or excessive fatigue.

Recovery is part of the plan. Sleep, nutrition, hydration, and sensible scheduling all influence how the crew responds. A good plan is reviewed and adjusted rather than copied unchanged from another person.
lessons.key_takeaway: Progression must be paired with recovery and individual review.

key_points: Frequency, intensity, time, type, and progression guide exercise design.
Station plans combine resistance and aerobic work.
Exercise scheduling commonly includes about two hours per day including setup.
Individualization, recovery, and review are essential.

practical_activity.title: Balance the Week
practical_activity.prompt: Outline a one-week exercise framework with both resistance and aerobic sessions, plus one recovery day.
steps: Choose a realistic number of sessions for a busy crew schedule.
Alternate or combine resistance and aerobic work.
Include a recovery and review point.
Explain one way you would individualize the plan.

questions.question: What does progression mean in an exercise plan?
options: Increasing challenge gradually as capacity improves
Doing the same session forever
Skipping recovery
Changing every variable every day
questions.explanation: Progression is a gradual increase in challenge, paired with adequate recovery.

questions.question: Why does a station exercise plan include both resistance and aerobic work?
options: They support different body systems and mission capabilities
One is always optional
Aerobic work only affects mood
Resistance work only affects sleep
questions.explanation: Resistance supports bone and muscle; aerobic supports cardiovascular fitness. Both are valuable.

questions.question: What is a realistic statement about exercise time on the station?
options: Exercise takes no scheduled time
NASA schedules substantial daily exercise time, often around two hours including setup
Exercise is only done once a month
Exercise is optional for all crew members
questions.explanation: Exercise is a scheduled countermeasure. NASA commonly describes about two hours per day including setup, while individual plans vary.

questions.question: Why should an exercise plan be individualized?
options: Every crew member has different needs, history, and responses
Because equipment is never shared
Because exercise has no general principles
To make scheduling harder
questions.explanation: Individual health status, experience, and response influence the appropriate plan.

modules.title: Injury Prevention and Team Safety
modules.summary: How crews prevent exercise injury and respond to equipment problems.

lessons.title: Preventing Injury
content: Injury prevention starts before the session: correct restraints, a clear area, appropriate load, and a warm-up. Technique matters, especially when the body is adapting to weightlessness and equipment behaves differently.
Crew members should stop if they feel sharp pain, unusual instability, or a device malfunction. Reporting is a safety action, not a failure. The team can then adjust the plan and arrange inspection.
lessons.key_takeaway: Preparation, technique, and early reporting prevent small problems from becoming mission-limiting ones.

lessons.title: Team Safety and Equipment Faults
content: A crew member using a faulty device is not the only person at risk. A fault can reduce exercise options for everyone, disrupt the schedule, and create pressure to skip the countermeasure.

The safe response is coordinated: stop use, secure the equipment, notify the team, document the fault, use approved alternatives, and schedule maintenance. Team safety depends on clear roles and honest reporting.
lessons.key_takeaway: A fault is managed by the team through stopping, documenting, substituting, and repairing.

key_points: Warm-up, restraints, area checks, and appropriate load reduce injury risk.
Sharp pain, instability, or equipment abnormality should stop a session.
Equipment faults affect the whole crew's exercise options.
Stop use, document, substitute approved activity, and repair.

practical_activity.title: Fault Response Drill
practical_activity.prompt: Write a five-step team response to a suspected exercise equipment fault.
steps: Make the immediate safety call.
Protect the equipment and the crew.
Notify, document, substitute, and schedule repair.

questions.question: What is the first priority when a crew member reports sharp pain during exercise?
options: Finish the session to avoid losing time
Stop the activity and assess the situation
Increase the load to test the pain
Ignore it if the crew member is experienced
questions.explanation: Stopping and assessing is the safe first step. The cause may require follow-up and plan adjustment.

questions.question: Why is prompt reporting of an equipment fault important?
options: It protects the crew and preserves the exercise plan
It guarantees the device will not break
It replaces maintenance
It is only needed for record keeping
questions.explanation: Early reporting allows the team to stop use, substitute activity, and repair before the problem worsens.

questions.question: Which is an approved way to maintain exercise during a device repair?
options: Use the faulty device at full load
Use approved alternative exercise options while the device is serviced
Skip exercise entirely
Ask the crew to invent a new device
questions.explanation: Approved alternatives preserve the countermeasure while the faulty device is unavailable.

questions.question: What makes an exercise safety culture strong?
options: Blaming crew members who report faults
Clear procedures, no-blame reporting, and consistent follow-through
Skipping warm-ups to save time
Using equipment without restraints
questions.explanation: Clear procedures and psychological safety encourage early reporting and consistent risk reduction.

practical_activity.title: Build a Weekly Microgravity Exercise Circuit
practical_activity.description: Design a one-week exercise framework for a station crew. Use approved equipment concepts and qualitative exercise principles. Do not present it as a personalized medical prescription.
steps: Include warm-up, aerobic work, resistance work, mobility, and recovery.
Explain how you would use the resistance device, treadmill with harness, and cycle ergometer.
Include a backup plan for one equipment fault.
Explain how sleep and nutrition support recovery.
Describe how you would individualize and review the plan.
practical_activity.submission_prompt: Paste your weekly framework and rationale. Explain how it protects bone, muscle, cardiovascular fitness, and crew safety.

questions.question: A crew member's resistance device feels abnormal. What is the best first action?
options: Complete the session and report it tomorrow
Stop, secure the device, and report the fault while using approved alternatives
Increase the load to see if it resolves
Ask the crew member to repair it without procedures
questions.explanation: Suspected equipment faults require stopping use, documentation, approved substitutions, and maintenance.

questions.question: Which combination best protects bone and muscle in microgravity?
options: Adequate loading through resistance exercise plus nutrition and recovery
Only passive stretching
Cutting calories to reduce body mass
Avoiding all exercise to prevent injury
questions.explanation: Bone and muscle benefit from loading, supported by nutrition and recovery.

questions.question: Why is a two-hour exercise allocation often discussed for station crews?
options: Exercise is a major countermeasure and setup takes time
Exercise is a leisure activity with no safety role
It guarantees no bone loss
It replaces sleep
questions.explanation: Exercise is a scheduled countermeasure. The time includes exercise and related setup, though individual plans vary.

questions.question: What is the best way to handle reduced exercise during an equipment fault?
options: Abandon all exercise and nutrition planning
Use approved alternatives and adjust nutrition to support recovery
Double the remaining sessions without progression
Ignore the fault until the end of the mission
questions.explanation: Approved alternatives keep the countermeasure going, and nutrition supports recovery during the disruption.

questions.question: Which statement about exercise prescription is most accurate?
options: One plan is perfect for every astronaut
A plan uses general principles but is individualized and reviewed
Exercise should always be maximal
Recovery is optional
questions.explanation: General principles guide planning, but individual needs and responses require review and adjustment.

questions.question: What is the strongest safety response to a crew member reporting instability during a session?
options: Encourage them to finish
Stop the session, check the setup and equipment, and assess before continuing
Remove the restraints
Increase the load gradually
questions.explanation: Instability may indicate a setup, equipment, or health issue. Stopping to assess is the safe response.

badge.name: Fitness Officer
badge.description: Completed all Physical Health & Exercise requirements and passed the final assessment.

courses.title: Nutrition & Diet
courses.tagline: Fuel the crew, support adaptation, and make every meal count.
introduction: Food in space is life support, medicine, morale, and mission logistics at the same time. The crew needs enough energy and the right nutrients to support bone, muscle, cardiovascular health, and recovery.
This course covers the space food system, energy and macronutrients, micronutrients, hydration and water recovery, and the practical work of menu planning and food safety.
objectives: Describe the constraints that shape the space food system.
Explain the roles of energy, protein, carbohydrate, fat, vitamins, minerals, and water.
Apply nutrition reasoning to reduced exercise and bone health.
Build a realistic menu plan with variety, inventory awareness, and food-safety practices.

modules.title: The Space Food System
modules.summary: Why space food is engineered, packaged, and planned differently from food on Earth.

lessons.title: Food That Works in Orbit
content: Space food must be safe, stable, easy to handle in weightlessness, and practical to store. Common forms include thermostabilized pouches, freeze-dried foods, and shelf-stable items. Fresh foods may be available occasionally but are limited by shelf life and transportation.

Crumbs are a hazard because they can float into equipment and eyes. Packaging and preparation are designed to keep food contained. Rehydration and heating must fit the station's systems and crew time.
lessons.key_takeaway: Space food must be safe, contained, shelf-stable, and practical for the crew to prepare.

lessons.title: Menu Variety and Morale
content: A menu can meet nutrient needs and still fail if the crew will not eat it. Variety, familiar foods, cultural preferences, and flavor all affect intake and morale.
Menu fatigue can develop when the same items repeat. A good food plan rotates options and includes crew input while staying within the real constraints of storage and supply.
lessons.key_takeaway: Nutrition planning must consider acceptability and morale, not just nutrient content.

key_points: Space food is engineered for safety, shelf life, containment, and preparation.
Crumbs and floating food can damage equipment or cause injury.
Variety, familiarity, and crew preference influence intake.
Menu fatigue is a real planning concern.

practical_activity.title: Space Food Constraints
practical_activity.prompt: Choose three foods you enjoy and explain how each would need to be adapted for a station food system.
steps: Consider packaging, crumbs, shelf life, and preparation.
Identify which food would be easiest and which would be hardest.
Suggest one acceptable alternative for the hardest food.

questions.question: Why are crumbs a concern in space food systems?
options: They make the station colder
They can float into equipment, eyes, and air systems
They increase radiation
They reduce water recovery
questions.explanation: In weightlessness, crumbs do not fall. They can float into sensitive areas and create hazards.

questions.question: Which is a common characteristic of space food?
options: It must be shelf-stable and practical to prepare
It must always be fresh
It must be liquid only
It must be high in salt
questions.explanation: Shelf stability, packaging, and practical preparation are core constraints.

questions.question: Why does menu variety matter?
options: It supports intake, morale, and reduces menu fatigue
It makes food less safe
It removes the need for nutrients
It reduces crew sleep
questions.explanation: Variety and preference influence how much and how well the crew eats.

questions.question: What is the best description of space food planning?
options: A purely financial decision
A balance of nutrition, safety, storage, preparation, and crew acceptability
A choice based only on flavor
A system that ignores shelf life
questions.explanation: Food planning integrates many constraints, including nutrition and acceptability.

modules.title: Energy and Macronutrients
modules.summary: How energy balance, protein, carbohydrate, and fat support the crew.

lessons.title: Energy Balance
content: The body needs enough energy for maintenance, activity, and recovery. In space, energy needs can be influenced by body size, exercise, workload, and individual metabolism. Undereating can undermine muscle, bone, immune function, and mood.
Energy balance is not about eating as little as possible. A crew member who is losing needed mass or feeling persistently fatigued needs a nutrition review, not a stricter restriction.
lessons.key_takeaway: Adequate energy is essential; cutting food is not a generic fix for reduced activity.

lessons.title: Protein, Carbohydrate, and Fat
content: Protein provides amino acids for tissue maintenance and repair. Carbohydrate supports energy needs, including during exercise. Fat is energy-dense and helps with nutrient absorption and food acceptability.

The right balance depends on the individual and the mission phase. A helpful educational rule is to avoid extremes and to connect macronutrient choices to the crew's actual workload, exercise plan, and health monitoring.
lessons.key_takeaway: Macronutrients support different functions; balance and adequacy matter more than a single number.

key_points: Energy needs vary with body size, activity, workload, and individual factors.
Undereating can harm muscle, bone, immunity, and mood.
Protein supports tissue maintenance and repair.
Carbohydrate and fat support energy and nutrient needs.

practical_activity.title: Build a Balanced Plate
practical_activity.prompt: Plan one station meal that includes a protein source, an energy source, a fruit or vegetable option, and a hydration component.
steps: Name each component and its role.
Explain how the meal stays contained and practical.
Suggest a variation to reduce menu fatigue.

questions.question: Why is cutting portions a poor response to reduced exercise?
options: The crew still needs adequate energy for health and recovery
Food has no effect on health
Exercise is the only factor in energy needs
Portions are unrelated to nutrition
questions.explanation: Reduced exercise does not automatically mean reduced nutritional needs. Adequacy and individual assessment matter.

questions.question: What is a primary role of protein?
options: Tissue maintenance and repair
Replacing sleep
Providing radiation shielding
Increasing cabin pressure
questions.explanation: Protein supplies amino acids used for tissue maintenance and repair.

questions.question: Which statement about energy needs is most accurate?
options: They are identical for every crew member
They vary with body size, activity, workload, and individual factors
They are only determined by sleep
They do not change during a mission
questions.explanation: Energy needs are individual and can change with workload and mission phase.

questions.question: What is the best nutrition principle during a workload change?
options: Maintain adequacy and review the plan with the crew
Always cut calories
Skip meals to save time
Rely only on snacks
questions.explanation: Adequacy and review are more useful than a blanket restriction.

modules.title: Micronutrients, Bone, and Vision
modules.summary: The supporting nutrients behind bone health, adaptation, and crew monitoring.

lessons.title: Calcium, Vitamin D, and Bone
content: Bone health depends on mechanical loading, hormones, and nutrients including calcium and vitamin D. In spaceflight, exercise and nutrition are both part of the countermeasure plan.

Vitamin D is important for calcium regulation and bone health. Crew nutrition plans include attention to micronutrients, and individual medical monitoring determines whether any supplement or adjustment is appropriate.
lessons.key_takeaway: Bone protection combines load, calcium, vitamin D, and individual medical monitoring.

lessons.title: Iron, Sodium, and Vision Monitoring
content: Iron supports oxygen transport, and sodium influences fluid balance. Spaceflight can affect how the body handles iron and sodium, so nutrition is part of the broader health picture rather than a set of isolated targets.

Some astronauts experience vision and eye changes during long-duration spaceflight. Nutrition may be part of the research picture, but no crew member should self-diagnose or self-treat. Changes are monitored by medical teams.
lessons.key_takeaway: Micronutrients matter, but eye and health changes require professional monitoring, not self-diagnosis.

key_points: Calcium and vitamin D support bone health.
Exercise and nutrition are combined countermeasures.
Iron and sodium are part of fluid and blood-health monitoring.
Vision changes in spaceflight require medical follow-up, not self-treatment.

practical_activity.title: Nutrient Support Map
practical_activity.prompt: Create a map linking bone health, oxygen transport, and fluid balance to at least one nutrient and one non-nutrition factor.
steps: Choose calcium, iron, and sodium.
Link each to a body function.
Add exercise, sleep, or medical monitoring as a supporting factor.

questions.question: Which nutrients are most directly associated with bone health?
options: Calcium and vitamin D
Caffeine and sugar
Sodium and chlorine only
Protein and water only
questions.explanation: Calcium and vitamin D support bone health, along with loading and other factors.

questions.question: What is the best response to a crew member who reports vision changes?
options: Tell them to self-treat with supplements
Document the change and refer to the medical monitoring process
Ignore it until the mission ends
Restrict all fluids
questions.explanation: Vision changes require professional monitoring. Self-diagnosis and self-treatment are unsafe.

questions.question: Why is bone protection more than a calcium supplement?
options: Bone also responds to mechanical loading and other health factors
Calcium has no role in bone
Supplements replace exercise
Bone health is unrelated to nutrition
questions.explanation: Bone health integrates loading, nutrition, hormones, and individual factors.

questions.question: What is a reasonable role for iron in crew health?
options: It supports oxygen transport and is part of blood-health monitoring
It replaces exercise
It controls cabin pressure
It prevents all radiation effects
questions.explanation: Iron is essential for oxygen transport. Spaceflight can affect iron metabolism, so monitoring matters.

modules.title: Hydration and Water Recovery
modules.summary: Why water balance and water recovery are central to crew health and station operations.

lessons.title: Water in the Body
content: Water supports circulation, temperature regulation, digestion, and cellular function. Hydration needs vary with activity, environment, and individual factors. In space, fluid shifts and station conditions can change how the crew feels and what they need.
A hydration plan should be practical: accessible water, regular reminders, and attention to signs of inadequate intake. It is not a competition to drink the most water.
lessons.key_takeaway: Hydration is individual and operational; regular access and attention matter more than a universal target.

lessons.title: Recovery and Reuse
content: The station's water recovery system helps reclaim water from sources such as humidity condensate and hygiene use. Recovery reduces the need for resupply, but it requires monitoring, maintenance, and crew discipline.

Drinking water and hygiene water are managed within the same broader system. Using water carelessly for hygiene can affect the shared supply. The correct operational response is to follow procedures, report anomalies, and coordinate demand.
lessons.key_takeaway: Water recovery is a shared system; hygiene and drinking needs must be coordinated.

key_points: Hydration supports circulation, temperature regulation, digestion, and cellular function.
Needs vary by activity, environment, and individual factors.
Water recovery reduces resupply needs but requires monitoring and discipline.
Hygiene and drinking water are part of a shared operational system.

practical_activity.title: Hydration and Recovery Plan
practical_activity.prompt: Design a one-day hydration reminder plan that also respects water recovery constraints.
steps: Choose three reminder points across the day.
Include one way to check that water is accessible and safe.
Describe how you would coordinate a hygiene block with the shared system.

questions.question: Why is hydration important for crew health?
options: It supports circulation, temperature regulation, and cellular function
It replaces sleep
It prevents all bone loss
It removes the need for food
questions.explanation: Water is involved in many core physiological functions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of water recovery on the station?
options: To reclaim water and reduce resupply needs
To create food
To increase radiation
To replace exercise
questions.explanation: Recovery systems reclaim water from station sources, reducing the need to launch all water from Earth.

questions.question: Why should hygiene water use be coordinated with the water system?
options: Hygiene and drinking water are part of a shared operational system
Hygiene has no effect on water
Drinking water is unrelated to recovery
Coordination is only for appearance
questions.explanation: Shared water systems require coordination to protect both hygiene and drinking needs.

questions.question: Which hydration approach is most reasonable?
options: Drink as much as possible at one time
Use regular access and reminders, and monitor individual needs
Avoid water to save the system
Rely only on caffeine
questions.explanation: Regular access and attention to individual needs are practical. Extremes are not helpful.

modules.title: Menu Planning, Variety, and Food Safety
modules.summary: Turning nutrition principles into a workable, safe, and acceptable menu.

lessons.title: From Inventory to Menu
content: Menu planning starts with what is actually available. A verified inventory prevents the plan from depending on items that are missing. Perishable or time-limited items should be used in a sensible order.
A good rotation balances nutrition, variety, crew preference, and preparation time. Involving the crew improves acceptability, but the final plan still has to meet safety and resource constraints.
lessons.key_takeaway: Build the menu on verified inventory, then balance nutrition, variety, preference, and time.

lessons.title: Food Safety and Sanitation
content: Food safety includes clean preparation surfaces, proper handling, and attention to package integrity. In a closed environment, a foodborne illness can affect the whole crew and the mission.

Crew members should report compromised packaging or unusual food condition. Cleaning routines and hand hygiene support food safety, and the same discipline protects the station's microbial environment.
lessons.key_takeaway: Food safety is crew safety: clean handling, intact packaging, and prompt reporting.

key_points: Verify inventory before finalizing a menu.
Use time-limited items in a sensible order.
Balance nutrition, variety, preference, and preparation time.
Clean handling and package integrity protect the crew.

practical_activity.title: Three-Day Menu Rotation
practical_activity.prompt: Create a three-day menu rotation using only foods you can reasonably assume are available in a station pantry. Include variety and a food-safety note.
steps: List the assumed available items.
Build three days with different combinations.
Identify which items should be used first.
Add one food-safety and one hydration note.

questions.question: What is the first step in a reliable menu plan?
options: Verify what is actually available
Choose only desserts
Ignore shelf life
Order food that has not arrived
questions.explanation: Verified inventory prevents the plan from relying on missing items.

questions.question: Why is food safety especially important in a closed station?
options: A foodborne illness can affect the whole crew and mission
There are no cleaning supplies
Food cannot be stored
Illness is impossible in space
questions.explanation: A confined crew shares risk. Prevention and prompt reporting are critical.

questions.question: Which factor should be balanced with nutrition in a menu plan?
options: Variety, preference, preparation time, and resources
Only color
Only cost
Nothing else
questions.explanation: A menu must be acceptable and practical as well as nutritious.

questions.question: What should a crew member do if a food package is compromised?
options: Eat it quickly
Report it and follow food-safety procedures
Mix it with another food
Ignore the package
questions.explanation: Compromised packaging is a safety issue and should be reported.

practical_activity.title: Plan a Three-Day Crew Menu
practical_activity.description: Create a three-day menu for a station crew using verified inventory assumptions, variety, hydration, and food-safety reasoning. Do not invent precise nutrient measurements.
steps: List the foods and drinks you assume are available.
Build three days of meals with variety and crew acceptability in mind.
Explain how the menu supports energy, protein, bone health, and hydration.
Identify time-limited items and a use-first plan.
Add food-safety and inventory-verification notes.
practical_activity.submission_prompt: Paste your three-day menu and rationale. Explain how you would adjust it if exercise is reduced or an inventory item is missing.

questions.question: A crew reduces exercise because of an equipment fault. What is the best nutrition response?
options: Cut all portions to match the lower activity
Maintain adequate energy and hydration, and emphasize supportive nutrients
Skip meals to save food
Increase only caffeine
questions.explanation: Reduced exercise does not justify cutting needed nutrition. Adequacy and supportive nutrients remain important.

questions.question: Why is inventory verification part of nutrition planning?
options: It prevents the menu from relying on items that are not available
It replaces food safety
It measures radiation
It makes food taste better
questions.explanation: A menu built on unverified stock is unreliable. Verification supports realistic planning.

questions.question: Which pair best supports bone health in spaceflight?
options: Mechanical loading and adequate calcium and vitamin D
Caffeine and reduced sleep
Skipping meals and avoiding exercise
High sodium and low hydration
questions.explanation: Bone health combines loading, nutrition, and medical monitoring.

questions.question: What is the best way to handle a food package that looks damaged?
options: Eat it and monitor for symptoms
Report it and follow food-safety procedures
Share it with the crew
Store it for later
questions.explanation: Damaged packaging is a potential safety issue and should be reported.

questions.question: Why does menu variety matter operationally?
options: It supports intake and morale and reduces menu fatigue
It makes food unsafe
It replaces hydration
It removes the need for inventory
questions.explanation: Crews eat better when menus are acceptable and varied, which supports nutrition and morale.

questions.question: Which statement about water recovery is most accurate?
options: It is unrelated to hygiene
It is a shared system that needs monitoring, maintenance, and coordinated use
It removes the need for hydration planning
It only applies to drinking water
questions.explanation: Water recovery supports multiple uses and requires disciplined shared operation.

courses.title: Mental Health & Psychology
courses.tagline: Support the human side of mission performance: trust, communication, and resilience.
introduction: A crew can have excellent hardware and still struggle if communication, workload, or morale break down. Spaceflight psychology is about supporting people in an isolated, confined, and demanding environment.
This course examines mission stressors, team communication, emotion regulation, workload and rest, and the support systems that help crews perform and stay well.
objectives: Identify common psychological stressors of spaceflight without diagnosing individuals.
Describe communication practices that support team cohesion and psychological safety.
Explain healthy coping and emotion-regulation strategies.
Design a crew care plan with check-ins, privacy, and escalation pathways.

modules.title: Stressors of Spaceflight
modules.summary: Why isolation, confinement, workload, and uncertainty affect crew performance.

lessons.title: The Environment
content: Space crews live in a small, technically complex environment with limited privacy and a fixed set of people. They are far from home, exposed to operational risk, and dependent on each other for safety.
Isolation and confinement can amplify ordinary frustrations. Noise, disrupted sleep, and a dense schedule add load. These are environmental stressors, not evidence that a crew member is weak.
lessons.key_takeaway: The mission environment creates predictable stressors that affect everyone.

lessons.title: Uncertainty and Meaning
content: Uncertainty about schedules, events, and performance can be more draining than a known challenge. Crew members may also feel the weight of being far from family or of representing a mission.
Support starts with acknowledging the reality of these pressures. Clear information, meaningful work, connection with home, and predictable routines help people maintain a sense of control.
lessons.key_takeaway: Clear information and connection help crews manage uncertainty.

key_points: Isolation, confinement, and limited privacy are environmental stressors.
Noise, sleep disruption, and workload add to the load.
Uncertainty can be more stressful than a known challenge.
Support begins with acknowledgment and practical structure.

practical_activity.title: Stressor Inventory
practical_activity.prompt: List four stressors a station crew might face and one practical support for each.
steps: Choose environmental, workload, communication, and family-related stressors.
For each, name a support that is realistic in a confined setting.
Avoid medical labels or diagnoses.

questions.question: Which is an environmental stressor of spaceflight?
options: Isolation and limited privacy
Unlimited access to family
A completely quiet station
An absence of scheduled tasks
questions.explanation: Isolation, confinement, and limited privacy are recognized stressors of the spaceflight environment.

questions.question: Why can uncertainty be stressful?
options: It reduces a person's sense of control and predictability
It always improves performance
It removes the need for communication
It makes sleep unnecessary
questions.explanation: Uncertainty can undermine a sense of control. Clear information and routines help.

questions.question: What is a helpful response to a crew member who is frustrated by confinement?
options: Dismiss the concern as weakness
Acknowledge it and look for practical ways to restore control and privacy
Assign more tasks
Tell them not to speak about it
questions.explanation: Acknowledgment plus practical support is more effective than dismissal.

questions.question: Which statement avoids diagnosing a crew member?
options: You have a disorder
You seem more withdrawn than usual; can we check in and review workload?
You are unfit for spaceflight
Your personality is the problem
questions.explanation: Describe observable changes and offer support without assigning a clinical label.

modules.title: Communication and Team Cohesion
modules.summary: How clear, respectful communication protects performance in a confined crew.

lessons.title: A Shared Mental Model
content: A crew performs best when members share an understanding of the plan, roles, and risks. Briefings, read-backs, and explicit task ownership reduce assumptions.
Communication is not only about transmitting facts. Tone, timing, and whether people feel safe to speak up affect whether important information reaches the team.
lessons.key_takeaway: Shared understanding and psychological safety are operational assets.

lessons.title: Conflict and Repair
content: Conflict is normal in a close team. The risk is not disagreement itself; it is unresolved disagreement that becomes avoidance, silence, or passive resistance.
A short facilitated conversation can clarify interests, separate people from the problem, and agree on next steps. Follow-up matters because a single conversation may not repair trust.
lessons.key_takeaway: Address conflict early with structure and follow-up rather than avoidance.

key_points: Shared mental models reduce assumptions and errors.
Psychological safety helps crew members speak up.
Conflict is normal; unresolved conflict is the risk.
Facilitated conversation plus follow-up supports repair.

practical_activity.title: Briefing and Read-Back
practical_activity.prompt: Write a short briefing for a task handover, then design a read-back question that checks understanding.
steps: State the task, owner, timing, and one risk.
Ask a question that requires the listener to explain the plan in their own words.
Add one invitation for questions or concerns.

questions.question: What is a shared mental model?
options: A common understanding of the plan, roles, and risks
A type of station software
A medical diagnosis
A rule that only leaders speak
questions.explanation: A shared mental model helps the team coordinate without relying on assumptions.

questions.question: Why is psychological safety important for a crew?
options: It helps people speak up about risks and mistakes
It eliminates all conflict
It replaces task training
It guarantees perfect decisions
questions.explanation: People are more likely to report concerns when they feel safe from blame.

questions.question: What is the main risk of unresolved conflict?
options: It can lead to avoidance, silence, and degraded communication
It always improves team performance
It has no effect in a confined crew
It removes the need for briefings
questions.explanation: Unresolved conflict can damage information flow and trust, which affects safety.

questions.question: Which is a good conflict-response step?
options: Ignore it until the mission ends
Facilitate a conversation, clarify ownership, and schedule follow-up
Assign blame publicly
Separate the crew permanently
questions.explanation: Structured conversation and follow-up address the issue without escalating blame.

modules.title: Emotion Regulation and Coping
modules.summary: Practical strategies for managing stress without pretending it does not exist.

lessons.title: Name It to Manage It
content: Recognizing and naming an emotion can reduce its intensity and help a person choose a response. This is not about forcing positivity; it is about creating a little space between feeling and action.
Useful strategies include slow breathing, brief physical activity, journaling, talking with a trusted person, and breaking a large task into smaller steps. Different people prefer different tools.
lessons.key_takeaway: Naming a feeling and choosing a deliberate response is more effective than suppressing it.

lessons.title: Limits of Self-Help
content: Coping strategies are useful, but they are not a substitute for professional support when distress is persistent or affecting safety. A crew member who is not sleeping, withdrawing, or feeling unable to function needs a supportive escalation path.
Asking for help is a professional skill. A crew culture that treats support as normal is safer than one that expects people to hide struggle.
lessons.key_takeaway: Self-help has a place, but persistent distress requires professional support.

key_points: Naming emotions can support regulation.
Breathing, movement, journaling, and connection are practical tools.
Coping strategies are not a substitute for professional care.
Asking for help is a professional skill.

practical_activity.title: Personal Coping Menu
practical_activity.prompt: Create a three-item coping menu for a stressful moment, plus one signal that would prompt you to seek support.
steps: Choose one body-based, one cognitive, and one social strategy.
Describe when each is useful.
Name a signal that self-help is not enough.

questions.question: What is a healthy purpose of naming an emotion?
options: To create space for a deliberate response
To eliminate all feelings
To prove a person is weak
To avoid communication
questions.explanation: Naming can reduce intensity and support a chosen response.

questions.question: Which is a practical coping strategy?
options: Slow breathing and breaking a task into smaller steps
Ignoring persistent distress
Hiding all concerns from the team
Working without rest
questions.explanation: Breathing and task chunking are practical regulation tools.

questions.question: When is self-help not enough?
options: When distress is persistent or affecting safety and function
Whenever a person feels tired
Only after the mission ends
Never
questions.explanation: Persistent distress or functional impairment calls for professional support.

questions.question: What does a healthy crew culture say about asking for help?
options: It is a professional skill and should be normalized
It is a sign of failure
It should be punished
It should only happen after an error
questions.explanation: Normalizing support encourages early action and reduces risk.

modules.title: Workload, Rest, and Fatigue
modules.summary: Balancing demands and resources to protect performance and well-being.

lessons.title: Demands and Resources
content: Workload is a relationship between demands and resources. High demand can be manageable with adequate time, support, control, and rest. The same demand can become harmful when those resources are missing.
Crews often face both overload and monotony. Long periods of monitoring can be tiring in a different way from a burst of intense work. Both require thoughtful scheduling.
lessons.key_takeaway: Workload risk depends on demands relative to time, support, control, and rest.

lessons.title: Rest and Recovery
content: Rest is not only sleep. Breaks, changes of task, connection with home, and moments of privacy help people recover. A schedule that leaves no room for any of these can erode performance.
The crew and operations team should review workload regularly. If fatigue or distress is rising, the plan needs a real adjustment, not just an encouragement to try harder.
lessons.key_takeaway: Recovery needs schedule space and real adjustments, not just encouragement.

key_points: Workload is demands relative to resources.
Both overload and monotony can increase risk.
Rest includes breaks, privacy, connection, and sleep.
Regular review should lead to real schedule adjustments.

Any task that requires concentration
A schedule with breaks

options: Make a real schedule or support adjustment
Tell the crew to try harder
Add more tasks

questions.explanation: Review should lead to action. Encouragement alone does not reduce risk.

modules.title: Behavioral Health Support and Monitoring
modules.summary: How crews and support teams promote well-being, privacy, and appropriate escalation.

lessons.title: Support That People Will Use
content: Behavioral health support includes regular check-ins, access to private conversations, sleep and workload review, and clear pathways for escalating a concern. It should be normalized as part of crew care.
Privacy and trust are essential. A crew member is more likely to use support if they believe concerns will be handled respectfully and not used against them.
lessons.key_takeaway: Accessible, private, and trusted support is more important than a policy on paper.

lessons.title: Monitoring Without Diagnosing
content: Crew monitoring looks for changes in sleep, mood, behavior, communication, and performance. The purpose is to offer support and adjust the mission plan, not to label a person.

When a concern exceeds the crew's ability to support, the team escalates through the appropriate medical and behavioral health channel. In this educational simulation, no real diagnosis or treatment is provided.
lessons.key_takeaway: Monitor for change, support early, and escalate appropriately without diagnosing.

key_points: Regular check-ins and private support should be normal crew care.
Privacy and trust determine whether support is used.
Monitoring looks for changes, not labels.

courses.title: Hygiene & Personal Care
courses.tagline: Protect health, dignity, and life support with smart personal care.
introduction: Hygiene in space is a life-support topic. Water is limited and recycled, surfaces are shared, and airflow behaves differently. Personal care routines must protect both the crew and the station systems.
This course covers water conservation, body and oral care without a shower, cleaning and microbial control, and the routines that support privacy and morale.
objectives: Explain why hygiene water must be coordinated with the station's recovery system.
Describe practical body, oral, and skin care approaches in microgravity.
Apply cleaning and airflow principles to shared station spaces.
Design a low-water personal care routine that respects privacy and crew preferences.

mission_links.label: Day 1 - Water Recovery and Hygiene Coordination

modules.title: Water: A Precious Resource
modules.summary: Why hygiene planning starts with the water system.

lessons.title: Every Drop Is Planned
content: Water on the station is used for drinking, food preparation, hygiene, and other operational needs. Recovery systems reclaim water from sources such as humidity condensate and used hygiene water, reducing how much must be launched from Earth.
Because the system is shared, a hygiene decision can affect the whole crew. Sequencing activities, using conservative techniques, and reporting anomalies are part of personal care.
lessons.key_takeaway: Hygiene water is part of a shared recovery system, not an unlimited personal supply.

lessons.title: Conservation Without Sacrifice
content: Conservation does not mean skipping hygiene. It means using methods that clean effectively with less water: wipes, rinse-free products, controlled dispensing, and reusable cloths where appropriate.
The goal is a sustainable routine that protects skin, mouth, and shared surfaces while keeping demand predictable. Crew members should know which products are approved for the station environment.
lessons.key_takeaway: The aim is effective, low-water hygiene, not zero hygiene.

key_points: Station water supports drinking, food, hygiene, and operations.
Recovery systems reclaim water and reduce resupply.
Hygiene demand is shared and must be coordinated.
Low-water methods can be effective when used correctly.

questions.question: What is the best description of water conservation in space?
options: Skipping all hygiene
Using effective low-water methods and coordinated demand
Using more water to save time
Ignoring the recovery system
questions.explanation: Conservation means maintaining effective hygiene with less water and predictable demand.

questions.question: Which source can water recovery systems reclaim water from?
options: Humidity condensate and used hygiene water
Only fresh Earth water
Only food packaging
Only urine from plants
questions.explanation: Recovery systems reclaim water from station sources such as condensate and hygiene water.

options: Ignore it and continue
Report it and follow the coordinated response
Use more water to flush it
Turn off all hygiene permanently
questions.explanation: Reporting and following procedures protect the crew and the system.

modules.title: Body Hygiene Without a Shower
modules.summary: How crews stay clean using wipes, rinse-free products, and controlled airflow.

lessons.title: Cleaning in Weightlessness
content: Water does not fall or pool in microgravity. Crews use rinse-free shampoo, body wipes, and cloths, then manage the used materials carefully. Airflow helps remove moisture and keep surfaces dry.
The goal is to clean the skin without leaving excess moisture in a closed environment. Products must be approved, and used wipes must be disposed of properly to avoid microbial growth.
lessons.key_takeaway: Low-water cleaning works when products, airflow, and waste handling are planned together.

lessons.title: Skin and Comfort
content: Skin can become dry or irritated in a closed, low-humidity environment. Gentle cleansing and moisturizing can help, but persistent rashes or irritation should be reported to the medical team.
Comfort and dignity matter. A predictable hygiene routine helps crew members feel human and maintain morale during a demanding mission.
lessons.key_takeaway: Skin care is both a health and a morale issue; persistent problems need medical review.

key_points: Water does not fall or pool in microgravity.
Rinse-free products, wipes, and airflow support body hygiene.
Used materials must be disposed of properly.
Persistent skin problems should be reported.
