questions.question: What is a useful body-cleaning method in microgravity?
options: Rinse-free products and wipes with controlled airflow
A full shower with open water
Using no cleaning products
Spraying water freely
questions.explanation: Rinse-free products, wipes, and airflow support hygiene without free water.

questions.question: Why must used wipes be managed carefully?
options: They can support microbial growth if left in the environment
They are food

They improve airflow

Report it for medical review and follow care guidance
Use more perfume
Stop all hygiene
questions.explanation: Persistent skin problems need medical review. Self-treatment can be unsafe.

modules.title: Oral and Skin Care
modules.summary: The small routines that protect health and comfort every day.

lessons.title: Oral Care in Orbit
content: Oral care follows familiar principles: brush, clean between teeth, and maintain regular routines. In microgravity, the challenge is managing water and foam without a sink that drains normally.
Crews use small amounts of water and approved products, then wipe or swallow safely according to procedures. Good oral care protects the crew from preventable dental problems during a mission.
lessons.key_takeaway: Oral care is familiar but must be adapted to manage water and foam.

lessons.title: Skin, Nails, and Grooming
content: Grooming is part of personal care and morale. Nail clippings and hair must be contained because loose material can float into eyes or equipment. Mirrors, lighting, and restraints help crew members groom safely.
Skin and nail changes should be monitored. A small problem can become more serious in a confined environment, so reporting is part of prevention.
lessons.key_takeaway: Contain loose material and report skin or nail changes early.

key_points: Oral care follows regular brushing and cleaning principles.
Water and foam must be managed without a normal sink.
Hair and nail clippings must be contained.
Skin and nail changes should be reported early.

options: Water and foam must be managed without a draining sink
Teeth do not need cleaning

modules.title: Cleaning, Air, and Microbial Control
modules.summary: How shared surfaces, airflow, and cleaning routines protect a closed environment.

lessons.title: A Shared Microbial Environment
content: A closed station contains people, surfaces, equipment, and airflow. Microorganisms travel on hands, droplets, and dust. Cleaning and hand hygiene reduce the chance that a small contamination becomes a shared problem.
Station teams monitor the microbial environment and follow cleaning schedules. Crew members support this by cleaning shared surfaces, handling waste correctly, and reporting spills or unusual growth.
lessons.key_takeaway: Cleaning is a shared responsibility in a closed environment.

lessons.title: Airflow and Filters
content: Airflow helps distribute air, remove moisture, and carry particles toward filters. Blocking vents or leaving wet materials in the open can undermine that system.
Filters and life-support equipment need maintenance. Crews should keep areas clear, follow stowage rules, and report unusual odors, condensation, or airflow changes.
lessons.key_takeaway: Keep airflow paths clear and report changes in moisture, odor, or airflow.

key_points: Microorganisms travel through a shared closed environment.
Hand hygiene and surface cleaning reduce contamination.
Airflow and filters need clear paths and maintenance.
Report spills, unusual growth, odors, or airflow changes.

modules.title: Personal Care Routines and Privacy
modules.summary: Designing routines that protect health, dignity, and crew cohesion.

lessons.title: Routine and Privacy
content: A predictable personal care routine helps crew members feel in control. Privacy is limited on a station, so schedules and designated areas matter. Crew members should be able to manage hygiene with reasonable dignity.
Preferences vary. A good plan respects individual needs while keeping shared resources and schedules workable. Small accommodations can have a meaningful effect on morale.
lessons.key_takeaway: Personal care planning should protect both resources and dignity.

lessons.title: Clothing and Shared Responsibilities
content: Clothing is limited and laundry is not like home. Crews manage clothing rotation, cleanliness, and stowage. Clean clothing and bedding support skin health and comfort.
Shared responsibilities such as cleaning schedules and supply tracking keep the environment functioning. Everyone contributes, and concerns should be raised before they become conflicts.
lessons.key_takeaway: Clothing, cleaning, and supply routines are shared crew responsibilities.

key_points: Predictable routines support a sense of control.
Privacy and dignity should be designed into hygiene schedules.

courses.title: Human Body in Microgravity
courses.tagline: Understand how the body adapts to weightlessness and returns to gravity.
introduction: Microgravity is not a single change; it is a whole-body experiment. Fluids shift, the vestibular system receives conflicting signals, the heart and blood vessels adapt, and bone and muscle lose loading.
This course explains the major adaptations, the difference between adaptation and disease, and why monitoring and reconditioning matter during and after spaceflight.
objectives: Describe the major physiological changes that occur in microgravity.
Explain headward fluid shift and space adaptation symptoms.
Connect cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, neuro-ocular, and immune changes to crew health.
Build an educational crew adaptation briefing that avoids diagnosis and invented measurements.

mission_links.label: Day 2 - Select a Radiation Protection Posture
Day 5 - Crew Health and Fitness Debrief

modules.title: Gravity and the Human Body
modules.summary: How gravity shapes the body and why removing it changes multiple systems.

lessons.title: A Body Built for Gravity
content: Human physiology is adapted to a gravity environment. Gravity influences how blood is distributed, how the skeleton is loaded, how balance is organized, and how movement is planned.

When gravity is removed, the body does not simply switch off. It begins a process of adaptation. Some changes are short-term adjustments; others become more pronounced during long-duration spaceflight.
lessons.key_takeaway: Microgravity triggers a coordinated adaptation across many body systems.

lessons.title: Adaptation Is Not Automatically Harmful
content: Some changes in space are normal adaptations to the environment. For example, the cardiovascular system may adjust its volume and the vestibular system may recalibrate. The operational concern is whether adaptation reduces capability during the mission or during return to gravity.
Monitoring helps the team distinguish expected adaptation from a concerning change. In this course, we describe patterns and support principles, not individual diagnoses.
lessons.key_takeaway: Distinguish expected adaptation from a change that needs medical review.

key_points: Gravity influences fluid distribution, bone, muscle, balance, and movement.
Microgravity produces a coordinated whole-body adaptation.
Some changes are expected adaptations; others require monitoring.
Educational content cannot replace medical assessment.

practical_activity.title: Gravity Systems Map

steps: Choose fluid distribution, bone and muscle, and balance.

questions.question: Why does microgravity affect multiple body systems?
options: Gravity influences fluid distribution, loading, balance, and movement
Only the muscles are affected
The body stops adapting

questions.question: Which statement is most accurate?
options: All changes in space are diseases

No changes occur in space
Adaptation never affects performance
questions.explanation: The course distinguishes expected adaptation from concerning change.

questions.question: What is the role of monitoring during adaptation?
options: To notice changes and support informed decisions
To replace all exercise
To label every crew member
To eliminate uncertainty
questions.explanation: Monitoring supports awareness and timely support, not labeling.

questions.question: Why is an educational course not a medical diagnosis?

Because monitoring is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Individual assessment requires qualified medical evaluation.

modules.title: Fluid Shifts and the Head
modules.summary: Why fluids move toward the head and how the body responds.

lessons.title: The Headward Shift
content: On Earth, gravity pulls body fluids downward. In microgravity, that pull is removed, so fluids shift toward the head and upper body. Crew members may notice facial puffiness, nasal congestion, or a feeling of fullness in the head.

The body begins to adjust fluid volume over time. These changes are part of the adaptation picture, but they can also interact with vision, sleep, and comfort. Monitoring helps the team understand the pattern.
lessons.key_takeaway: Removing gravity's downward pull shifts fluids toward the head and upper body.

lessons.title: Pressure and Vision Research
content: Researchers study how the headward fluid shift and pressure changes may relate to eye and vision changes in some astronauts. The exact mechanisms are still an active area of research.

Crew members do not diagnose themselves. Vision changes are documented and evaluated by medical teams. The educational takeaway is that fluid shift is a whole-body adaptation with effects beyond how the face looks.
lessons.key_takeaway: Fluid shift can affect comfort and vision, and vision changes need professional evaluation.

key_points: Gravity normally pulls fluids downward.
Microgravity causes a headward fluid shift.
Facial puffiness and congestion are common descriptions.
Vision changes require medical monitoring, not self-diagnosis.

questions.question: Which is a commonly described effect of headward fluid shift?
options: Facial puffiness or nasal congestion
Loss of all vision
Immediate bone fracture
Complete loss of hearing

It only affects appearance
It is unrelated to spaceflight
questions.explanation: Fluid shift and related vision changes are active research areas.

modules.title: Balance, Movement, and Space Adaptation
modules.summary: Why the vestibular system struggles at first and how crews adapt.

lessons.title: Conflicting Balance Signals
content: The vestibular system in the inner ear helps sense head position and motion. On Earth, it works with visual and body-position cues. In microgravity, those cues no longer agree in the usual way.

The brain receives conflicting information. Some crew members experience nausea, dizziness, or disorientation during the first days of spaceflight. This is often described as space adaptation syndrome, but individual symptoms need medical review.
lessons.key_takeaway: Microgravity creates sensory conflict that can cause temporary disorientation or nausea.

lessons.title: Moving Safely While Adapting
content: Crews use handrails, move slowly, and orient themselves deliberately while adapting. Visual cues and consistent reference points help. Tasks that require precise movement may need extra care early in the mission.
Adaptation is usually gradual, but the timeline varies. A crew member who feels unwell should report it and follow medical guidance rather than pushing through a risky task.
lessons.key_takeaway: Slow, deliberate movement and early reporting support safety during adaptation.

key_points: The vestibular system senses head position and motion.
Microgravity creates conflict between balance, visual, and body cues.
Nausea and disorientation can occur during adaptation.
Handrails, slow movement, and reporting support safety.

questions.question: Why can crew members feel disoriented early in spaceflight?

questions.explanation: Sensory systems that normally agree now provide conflicting information.

questions.question: Which is a safe movement strategy during adaptation?
options: Move quickly and ignore symptoms

Remove all restraints
Attempt complex tasks immediately
questions.explanation: Deliberate movement and stable references support safety while adapting.

questions.question: What should a crew member do if nausea or disorientation is affecting a task?
options: Push through the task
Stop, report it, and follow medical guidance
Hide it from the team
Increase task complexity
questions.explanation: Symptoms that affect task performance should be reported and managed.

questions.question: What is space adaptation syndrome?
options: A descriptive term for symptoms during adaptation to microgravity
A station power failure
A type of exercise device
A permanent diagnosis for every astronaut
questions.explanation: It describes a set of adaptation symptoms. Individual assessment still requires medical judgment.

modules.title: Cardiovascular and Musculoskeletal Adaptation
modules.summary: How the heart, blood vessels, bone, and muscle respond to unloading.

lessons.title: The Cardiovascular System
content: The cardiovascular system adapts to the changed fluid distribution and workload of spaceflight. Blood volume and heart function can change, and some crew members experience orthostatic intolerance after returning to gravity.
Exercise, hydration, and monitored reconditioning are part of the response. The goal is to maintain capability during the mission and support the return to gravity.
lessons.key_takeaway: Cardiovascular adaptation affects both the mission and the return to gravity.

lessons.title: Bone and Muscle
content: Reduced mechanical loading contributes to bone loss and muscle atrophy. Resistance exercise provides a loading stimulus, while aerobic exercise supports cardiovascular fitness. Nutrition supports the tissue-repair environment.
The changes vary by individual and mission duration. Monitoring, exercise, and nutrition are combined, and rehabilitation continues after return.
lessons.key_takeaway: Bone and muscle protection combines loading, nutrition, monitoring, and rehabilitation.

key_points: The cardiovascular system adapts to fluid and workload changes.
Orthostatic intolerance can occur after return to gravity.
Bone loss and muscle atrophy are linked to unloading.
Exercise, nutrition, monitoring, and rehabilitation are combined.

practical_activity.title: Return-to-Gravity Brief
practical_activity.prompt: Explain three ways the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems can be supported during and after spaceflight.
steps: Choose exercise, hydration, and monitored reconditioning.
Explain the purpose of each.
Add one reason individual variation matters.

questions.question: Why can orthostatic intolerance occur after returning to gravity?
options: The cardiovascular system has adapted to microgravity
The body has too much bone
Gravity disappears on Earth
The crew did not sleep
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular adaptation can make it harder to maintain blood pressure when standing again.

questions.question: What supports bone and muscle during spaceflight?
options: Resistance exercise, nutrition, and monitoring
Avoiding all movement
Cutting all protein
Sleeping more than 12 hours
questions.explanation: Loading through exercise, nutrition, and monitoring are combined countermeasures.

questions.question: Why does rehabilitation continue after return?
options: The body needs time to readapt to gravity
Rehabilitation is only for athletes
Gravity has no effect on the body
Exercise becomes unnecessary
questions.explanation: Readaptation to gravity takes time and may require monitored exercise and support.

questions.question: Which statement about individual variation is correct?
options: Every crew member adapts identically
Adaptation and recovery vary between individuals
Only mission duration matters
Monitoring is unnecessary because variation is small
questions.explanation: Individual responses differ, so monitoring and individualized plans matter.

modules.title: Neuro-ocular and Immune Changes; Return to Gravity
modules.summary: The research frontier: vision, immunity, and reconditioning after spaceflight.

lessons.title: Vision and the Brain
content: Some astronauts experience changes in vision and eye structure during long-duration spaceflight. Researchers use the term Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome, or SANS, to describe a pattern of findings that is still being studied.
The cause is not fully understood. Fluid shift, pressure, and individual factors are part of the research. Crew members undergo monitoring, and any change is evaluated by medical professionals.
lessons.key_takeaway: SANS is an active research area; vision changes require professional monitoring.

lessons.title: Immune Changes and Reconditioning
content: Spaceflight can be associated with changes in immune function, and some latent viruses can reactivate without causing illness. The practical takeaway is that crew health monitoring, sleep, nutrition, exercise, and hygiene all support resilience.
Returning to gravity is its own adaptation. Crews may experience balance, blood-pressure, and strength changes. A structured reconditioning plan helps the body rebuild capacity safely.
lessons.key_takeaway: Immune resilience and return-to-gravity recovery are supported by integrated crew health practices.

key_points: SANS describes a pattern of eye and vision findings under study.
The causes of vision changes are not fully understood.
Immune changes can occur; monitoring and healthy routines matter.
Return to gravity requires reconditioning and follow-up.

practical_activity.title: Crew Adaptation Briefing
practical_activity.prompt: Prepare a five-point briefing on fluid shift, balance, cardiovascular fitness, bone and muscle, and vision monitoring for a new crew.
steps: Use plain language and avoid diagnoses.
Include one monitoring action and one countermeasure for each area.
End with the importance of reporting changes.

questions.question: What is SANS?
options: A pattern of eye and vision findings in spaceflight that researchers are studying
A station exercise machine
A type of radiation shield
A confirmed cure for vision loss
questions.explanation: SANS describes a research pattern. It is not a self-diagnosis or a complete explanation.

questions.question: What is a reasonable statement about immune changes in spaceflight?
options: They can occur, and crew health practices support resilience
They never occur
They guarantee illness
They are unrelated to sleep or nutrition
questions.explanation: Immune changes are an area of research. Sleep, nutrition, exercise, and hygiene support overall resilience.

questions.question: Why is reconditioning important after return to gravity?
options: The body must readapt after microgravity
Gravity has no effect
Exercise should stop after landing
Vision changes are the only concern
questions.explanation: Balance, blood pressure, and strength may need structured recovery after return.

questions.question: What should a crew member do about a persistent vision change?
options: Report it for professional evaluation
Self-treat with unapproved supplements
Ignore it
Stop all exercise without advice
questions.explanation: Persistent vision changes require professional evaluation.

practical_activity.title: Create a Crew Adaptation Briefing
practical_activity.description: Prepare an educational briefing for a new crew on how the human body adapts to microgravity and returns to gravity. Keep it descriptive and non-clinical.
steps: Cover fluid shift, balance and movement, cardiovascular fitness, bone and muscle, and vision monitoring.

final_assessment.title: Human Body in Microgravity Final Assessment

questions.question: Why does headward fluid shift occur in microgravity?
options: Gravity no longer pulls fluids toward the feet
The body makes too much blood
The heart stops
The crew drinks too much water
questions.explanation: Removing gravity's downward pull allows fluids to redistribute toward the upper body.

questions.question: What is the best response to nausea and disorientation during early adaptation?
options: Push through complex tasks
Move deliberately, use references, and report symptoms that affect safety
Ignore all symptoms
Remove handrails
questions.explanation: Safe movement and reporting support adaptation and reduce risk.

questions.question: Which combination best supports bone and muscle during spaceflight?
options: Resistance exercise, nutrition, and monitoring
Complete bed rest
Cutting protein and calcium
Avoiding all loading
questions.explanation: Loading through exercise, nutrition, and monitoring are combined countermeasures.

questions.question: What is a responsible statement about SANS?
options: It is fully understood and easily self-treated
It is a research area involving eye and vision changes that requires professional monitoring
It has no effect on astronauts
It is caused only by exercise
questions.explanation: SANS is an active research area. Vision changes require professional evaluation.

questions.question: Why does return to gravity require reconditioning?
options: The body has adapted to microgravity and must readapt
Gravity is stronger than before
Exercise becomes harmful
The crew no longer needs sleep
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular, balance, and musculoskeletal systems need time to readapt.

questions.question: Which is the best overall approach to crew adaptation?
options: Monitor, support with exercise and nutrition, and report concerning changes
Ignore all changes until landing
Use unapproved treatments
Avoid all physical activity
questions.explanation: Integrated monitoring and support protect crew health across adaptation and return.

final_training_challenge.title: Final Training Challenge
final_training_challenge.subtitle: Integrated Crew Readiness Board
final_training_challenge.description: Bring the six Academy disciplines together in one final scenario. You will answer integrated questions and submit a Crew Readiness Brief that explains how you would support a crew across sleep, exercise, nutrition, mental health, hygiene, and microgravity adaptation.

practical_activity.title: Crew Readiness Brief
practical_activity.prompt: Write a concise brief for a crew preparing for a five-day station mission. Explain how you would support sleep, exercise, nutrition, mental health, hygiene, and human adaptation in microgravity. Identify one risk from each area and one practical countermeasure. End with how you would use the Academy knowledge during the mission simulation.

questions.question: A crew member has slept poorly for three nights and now reports irritability and slower reactions. What is the strongest first response?
options: Tell the crew member to use more caffeine and continue the schedule
Reduce nonessential workload, protect the next sleep opportunity, and check in again
Wait for the final assessment before making any change
Assume the behavior is a personality issue
questions.explanation: Cumulative fatigue affects performance and mood. The priority is to reduce risk, protect sleep, and follow up. Caffeine is not a substitute for recovery.

questions.question: A resistance exercise device behaves abnormally during a session. What should happen first?
options: Increase the load to test whether the fault clears
Continue the session and report the fault at the end of the week
Stop use, document the fault, and use approved alternatives while arranging inspection
Ask the crew to repair it without procedures
questions.explanation: Suspect hardware is removed from service and documented. Exercise continues through approved alternatives while the equipment is inspected.

questions.question: Exercise is temporarily reduced because of an equipment fault. How should nutrition change?
options: Cut meal portions so the crew eats less
Skip hydration to reduce water use
Maintain adequate energy and hydration, with attention to protein, calcium, and vitamin D
Replace meals with snacks only
questions.explanation: Reduced exercise does not mean cutting needed nutrition. Adequate intake and supportive nutrients remain important.

questions.question: During a solar particle event, what is the best combination of actions?
options: Continue all external work and delay communication until the event ends
Use shielding and time protection, pause nonessential work, and brief the crew clearly
Ignore the event because the station is always safe
Move the crew to the exercise area and increase workload
questions.explanation: Protection uses shielding, time, and distance. Clear communication reduces uncertainty, and nonessential work can wait.

questions.question: Water recovery is on watch while the crew wants to run a full hygiene block. What is the most responsible plan?
options: Run every hygiene task at once to finish quickly
Confirm the qualitative recovery status, sequence essential hygiene, and log use
Cancel all hygiene until the end of the mission
Use drinking water for cleaning without coordination
questions.explanation: Confirm status, sequence demand, and document use. Hygiene still matters, but it must be coordinated with the shared water system.

questions.question: Why do astronauts experience headward fluid shift in microgravity?
options: Gravity no longer pulls body fluids toward the feet
The body produces too much blood in space
The heart stops pumping blood
The crew is always dehydrated
questions.explanation: Without the usual downward pull of gravity, fluids shift toward the head and upper body. The body then adapts over time.

questions.question: Two crew members are in a persistent disagreement that is affecting communication. What is the best response?
options: Ignore it until the mission ends
Tell them to resolve it privately without support
Facilitate a short conversation with ground rules, clarify ownership, and schedule a follow-up
Move one crew member to a different mission permanently
questions.explanation: Facilitated communication addresses the issue while preserving psychological safety and team performance.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes NASA Mars Trek from a fictional mission scenario?
options: Mars Trek is a fictional game created for this platform
Mars Trek is an official NASA resource for exploring Mars data, while the station simulation is a fictional educational scenario
Both are official NASA operational tools
The simulation contains real operational procedures that can be used in spaceflight
questions.explanation: NASA Mars Trek is an official NASA resource. The five-day station mission is a fictional educational simulation and must be labeled as such.

questions.question: What belongs in an honest final mission handover?
options: Only the successful decisions
A summary of every day, the decision history, completed and pending tasks, and the final readiness picture
A list of tasks the next team should guess about
A promise that no risks remain
questions.explanation: A complete handover preserves the record, including open risks and unfinished tasks, so the next team can act responsibly.

questions.question: How should Academy learning connect to the mission simulator?
options: The Academy is optional and unrelated to mission decisions
Mission events should link to relevant Academy modules so knowledge can be applied to decisions
The simulator should replace all Academy content
Only the final assessment matters
questions.explanation: The Academy teaches the knowledge; the simulator tests application. Relevant mission events surface targeted learning recommendations.
